newsitem.title: UK: IPE pins Asia growth on Singapore as NYMEX expands.
newsitem.headline: IPE pins Asia growth on Singapore as NYMEX expands.

text.p: The International Petroleum Exchange is pinning its Asian growth on its fledgling Singapore Brent contract, even as the New York Mercantile Exchange, the oil market heavyweight, makes inroads in the continent.
"Currently the IPE is not in discussion with any other exchange in Asia," Richard Ward, director of IPE's business development division, told Reuters.
"For the moment our focus is on the SIMEX (Singapore International Monetary Exchange) where we believe our best opportunities lie for developing Brent as the international benchmark," he said.
He did not detail what measures were being taken to boost volume, but said the IPE and SIMEX are in talks aimed at "various initiatives" to encourage greater participation from the Far East.
"We do believe there is business in the Far East time zone and SIMEX has the opportunity to capture that," he said.

At the Asia-Pacific Petroleum Conference in Singapore this week, NYMEX announced plans to sign an agreement with the Hong Kong Futures Exchange that would allow its crude oil futures to be traded there by the first quarter of 1997.

Once the ACCESS, or electronic trading system, link is forged, it would take until at least early next year before trading could begin. It would be the second ACCESS centre in Asia after NYMEX set up a link with the Sydney Futures Exchange in September 1995.
NYMEX President Patrick Thompson said on Monday he hoped to resume talks with the SIMEX about setting up an ACCESS link in Singapore.

The U.S. exchange also said it was working to launch an Asia-specific futures energy contract to be traded on ACCESS, probably to be crude or gas oil based, with a cash, rather than delivery, settlement.
Officials said NYMEX was also exploring the potential for an ACCESS link in China sometime in the future.
"We don't consider it a lost opportunity for the IPE at this point," Ward said.
The Brent crude futures contract started trading on the SIMEX in June 1995 under the Mutual Offset System, but the IPE has openly expressed disappointment with its performance.
Still, Ward was optimistic because Singapore is the refining center for Asia and, he said, roughly 60 percent of the world's traded crudes are priced off of the Brent complex.
"We are disappointed with the current volumes quite clearly but the traded volumes that we saw during the recent crisis on the second and third of this month were far more encouraging," Ward said.
"But we would be looking for the contract to be consistently trading over 1,000 lots to be comfortable with its performance."
Year-to-date volume for the SIMEX Brent contract as of Sept 6 was 45,598, he said. Volume on Sept 2 and 3 jumped to 1,392 and 1,305 contracts, following U.S. missile attacks on Iraq.
